title: Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome
claims: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is a broad term for pain in the front of the knee and around the kneecap, sometimes called runner's knee; it is common in active people, especially females and young adults, but can also occur in nonathletes.
The most common symptom is a dull, aching pain in the front of the knee that begins gradually and is activity-related, affecting one or both knees.

PFPS pain occurs with repeated knee bending such as climbing stairs, running, jumping, or squatting, and after prolonged sitting with the knee bent; it may follow a change in activity level or intensity, playing surface, or equipment, and popping or crackling sounds may occur.
Most PFPS cases are treated nonsurgically: activity change to low-impact cycling, elliptical, or swimming; physical therapy focusing on quadriceps and hip strengthening; and sometimes shoe orthotics.
Surgical treatment for patellofemoral pain is very rarely needed and is performed only for severe cases that do not respond to nonsurgical treatment.

Prevention advice includes activity-appropriate shoes, a thorough warm-up, quadriceps and hamstring stretching, gradual increases in training intensity and duration, and maintaining a healthy body weight.
